topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: Under Wis. Stat. 700.17(1), when two or more persons own real estate concurrently, they may hold title as:
choice_a: Joint tenants or tenants in common
explanation: Wis. Stat. 700.17(1) recognizes two forms of concurrent ownership: joint tenancy and tenancy in common.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: Under Wis. Stat. 700.17(2)(a), each joint tenant's interest in the property is:
choice_a: Proportional to that tenant's financial contribution at creation
choice_b: Equal to every other joint tenant's interest, regardless of unequal contributions at creation
choice_c: Determined by a court at the time of sale
choice_d: Forfeited if the tenant fails to pay property taxes
explanation: Wis. Stat. 700.17(2)(a) provides that each joint tenant has an equal interest in the whole property for the duration of the tenancy, irrespective of unequal contributions at its creation.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: Under Wis. Stat. 700.17(2)(a), when one of two joint tenants dies, what happens to that tenant's interest?
choice_a: It passes through probate to the deceased tenant's heirs
choice_b: It is divided equally between the deceased tenant's heirs and the surviving tenant
choice_c: The surviving joint tenant automatically becomes the sole owner
choice_d: It reverts to the original grantor
explanation: Joint tenancy carries a right of survivorship: under Wis. Stat. 700.17(2)(a), when one of two joint tenants dies, the survivor automatically becomes the sole owner, bypassing probate for that interest.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: Under Wis. Stat. 700.17(3), a tenancy in common differs from a joint tenancy in that a tenant in common:
choice_a: Must hold an equal percentage interest to every other co-tenant
choice_b: Automatically inherits a deceased co-tenant's share
choice_c: Cannot convey their interest without the other co-tenants' consent
choice_d: Has an undivided interest in the whole property but with NO right of survivorship
explanation: Wis. Stat. 700.17(3) provides that each tenant in common has an undivided interest in the whole property, but there is no right of survivorship -- a deceased tenant in common's share passes through that owner's estate, not automatically to the co-owners.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: Under Wisconsin's Marital Property Act, Wis. Stat. 766.31(1)-(2), what is the general presumption regarding property acquired by a married couple?
choice_a: All property of spouses is presumed to be marital property, except property specifically classified otherwise
choice_b: All property automatically belongs to whichever spouse holds legal title
choice_c: Only property acquired before the marriage is presumed marital
choice_d: There is no presumption; each item must be individually litigated
explanation: Wis. Stat. 766.31(1)-(2) establishes that all property of spouses is marital property, and is presumed to be marital property, unless it is classified otherwise under ch. 766.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: Under Wis. Stat. 766.31(3), each spouse's interest in an item of marital property is:
choice_a: A future interest that vests only at divorce
choice_c: A 100% interest, held jointly with the other spouse
choice_d: Determined solely by which spouse earned the higher income
explanation: Wis. Stat. 766.31(3) gives each spouse a present, undivided one-half interest in each item of marital property.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: Under Wis. Stat. 766.31(7)(a), which of the following is classified as a spouse's individual (non-marital) property, rather than marital property?
choice_a: A salary earned during the marriage
choice_b: A home purchased jointly during the marriage
choice_c: Property acquired by gift or by a third person's disposition at death (inheritance)
choice_d: Rental income earned from a jointly owned property
explanation: Wis. Stat. 766.31(7)(a) classifies property acquired by gift during lifetime, or by a disposition at death by a third person (inheritance), as a spouse's individual property rather than marital property.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: Under Wis. Stat. 766.51(2), spouses who hold marital property in both of their names may manage and control that property:
choice_a: Independently, with either spouse able to convey it alone
choice_c: Only if a prenuptial agreement authorizes it
explanation: Wis. Stat. 766.51(2) requires spouses to act together to manage or control marital property that is held in both spouses' names -- the statutory reason both spouses' signatures are typically required to convey such property.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: Under Wis. Stat. 706.08(1)(a), an unrecorded conveyance of Wisconsin real estate is:
choice_a: Void as against a subsequent good-faith purchaser for value who records first
choice_b: Automatically void between the original parties
choice_c: Enforceable against everyone, recorded or not
choice_d: Valid only if witnessed by two people
explanation: Wis. Stat. 706.08(1)(a) makes an unrecorded conveyance void as against a subsequent good-faith purchaser for value who records first, even though it remains valid between the original parties.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: Wis. Stat. 706.09 protects a good-faith purchaser for value against certain stale, off-record defects in the chain of title. This statute is the reason Wisconsin title examination practice focuses primarily on:
explanation: Wis. Stat. 706.09 shields qualifying purchasers from certain stale claims based on defects not reflected in the recorded chain of title, which is why title examination in Wisconsin focuses on the recorded chain of title.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: A general warranty deed provides the grantee with the broadest protection because the grantor warrants title against:
choice_a: Only defects the grantor personally caused
choice_b: Only defects arising after the sale closes
choice_c: All defects in title, including those arising before the grantor's own period of ownership
choice_d: No defects; a general warranty deed carries no warranties
explanation: A general warranty deed is the broadest form of deed warranty, with the grantor warranting title against all defects, including those that arose before the grantor's own ownership of the property.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: A special (limited) warranty deed differs from a general warranty deed in that the grantor warrants title only against defects:
choice_a: Arising at any point in history, including before the grantor owned the property
choice_b: That the buyer later discovers within one year
choice_c: That are recorded in a different county
choice_d: Arising during the grantor's own period of ownership
explanation: A special (limited) warranty deed narrows the grantor's warranty to defects arising only during the grantor's own period of ownership, not defects that arose before the grantor acquired the property.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: A quitclaim deed conveys:
choice_a: Whatever interest the grantor actually has, if any, with no warranty of title at all
choice_c: Only a leasehold interest, never a fee simple interest
choice_d: Title free of all liens, regardless of what the grantor actually owns
explanation: A quitclaim deed conveys only whatever interest the grantor actually holds, if any, with no warranty of title -- it is commonly used to clear a cloud on title rather than in an arm's-length sale.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: In current Wisconsin real estate practice, evidence of title for a buyer (and the buyer's lender) is customarily provided through:
choice_a: A notarized affidavit from the seller alone
choice_b: An owner's (and lender's) title insurance policy issued after a search of the recorded chain of title
choice_c: A verbal assurance from the listing broker
choice_d: The property's original 19th-century abstract, updated by memory
explanation: Wisconsin practice customarily provides evidence of title through an owner's title insurance policy (and a lender's policy for the mortgagee), issued after a title search of the recorded chain of title, rather than the older abstract-and-attorney's-opinion method.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: "Involuntary alienation" of real property, a topic in the REEB 25.033(9) title-transfer curriculum, refers to a transfer of title:
choice_a: That the owner voluntarily negotiates and signs
choice_b: That only occurs when the owner dies without a will
choice_c: Without the owner's consent, such as through foreclosure, tax deed, eminent domain, or adverse possession
choice_d: That requires the owner's notarized signature
explanation: Involuntary alienation describes a transfer of title that occurs without the owner's consent, such as through foreclosure, a tax deed, eminent domain, or adverse possession -- in contrast to a voluntary conveyance the owner signs and delivers.

topic: Real Property Ownership, Estates & Title Transfer
question: When a property owner dies leaving a valid will, REEB 25.033(9)(e)'s curriculum topic of "transferring title by will" describes title passing to the beneficiaries through:
choice_a: An automatic, immediate transfer with no court involvement
choice_b: A quitclaim deed signed by the deceased's attorney
choice_c: The Real Estate Examining Board's approval
choice_d: The probate process, which validates the will and oversees distribution of the estate
explanation: Title passing under a will generally goes through probate, the court process that validates the will and oversees distribution of the deceased owner's estate to the named beneficiaries.
